passage: Nilesh, sit down, let old Sabina tell you something. When I finished my first portfolio I was proud for exactly one day. Then I scrolled through pages from the big technical institutes. Sleek animations, dark themes, projects with hundreds of users. I looked at mine and thought, "Nobody would want to see this." I closed the tab. For four months I told nobody it existed. Meanwhile a friend who had been on the same course got an internship with a much plainer page. When she finally saw mine, she said, "This is good. Why is it hiding?" I had no answer. The work was decent. I had only compared it with the wrong people, and the cost was four months of doors I never knocked on.

passage:
Chandrika had exactly one evening before the internship form closed, and the power in her rented room in Bhopal kept flickering. Her portfolio was ready: a crop-price dashboard, a hostel complaint tracker, and clean write-ups for both. Her classmate Asif had checked it that morning and said, 'Send it. It's good.'
At 8 p.m. she opened a few portfolios from students at the most famous institutes to 'just compare'. Dark themes, 3D animations, projects with thousands of users. By 9:30 she had scrolled through twenty. Her own site suddenly looked like a school notebook.
'It's not worth showing,' she typed to Asif.
'It's decent. Deadline's at midnight.'
The power went out at 11:15. She sat in the dark with her phone at eleven percent and did not open the form. The next morning Asif told her he'd been shortlisted with a site simpler than hers.

qa.q: How many portfolios had Chandrika scrolled through by 9:30?
What was Chandrika feeling after comparing her site with the others?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and inadequate, as though her decent work looked like a school notebook next to theirs.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Chandrika at 8 p.m.?
qa.a: Submit first, since Asif had already said it was good, and look at other portfolios later only for ideas.

qa.q: How might Asif feel about being shortlisted with a simpler site?
qa.a: Asif may feel sad for Chandrika, having told her it was good, knowing that her fear, not her work, kept her out.

grounding: Shows a student comparing a decent portfolio with polished ones from top institutes, deciding it is not worth showing, and missing a deadline.

passage:
On the local train back to his flat in Thane, Francis scrolled through portfolios that his classmate Manjula had shared in their group: students from famous institutes, with custom animations, published research and projects used across whole cities.
He had built a library seat-booking tool that sixty students at his college used every day. It had seemed like a lot on Monday.
'Did you post your link on the placement group?' Manjula asked the next day in the canteen.
'Not yet. It needs work.'
'What work?'
He couldn't name any. 'Compared to theirs, it's nothing.'
Two weeks passed. Manjula shared hers, found a mentor through the group, and got feedback. Francis kept tweaking colours at night and did not post. When a recruiter asked the group for portfolios, the thread closed before he had decided.

qa.q: How many students at Francis's college used the library seat-booking tool every day?
What does 'Compared to theirs, it's nothing' suggest about how Francis feels?
qa.a: He feels inadequate and behind, measuring a tool sixty students use against the most polished work he could find.

qa.q: What would you advise Francis when the comparing starts?
qa.a: Judge the tool by what it does for its sixty users, not by famous institutes, and post the link so real feedback can come in.

qa.q: How might Manjula see Francis's delay?
qa.a: Manjula likely feels puzzled and concerned, since sharing her own link brought a mentor and feedback while Francis stayed stuck.

grounding: Shows a student who, after scrolling polished portfolios from top institutes, feels decent work is not worth showing and keeps delaying.
